overview.title: What PolityMarket Measures
overview.text: This is not a poll or an election forecast. It’s a daily attempt to read the situation from public coverage.

mediaClimate.title: Media Tone
mediaClimate.text: This is the main indicator on screen. It shows whether today’s coverage appears positive, negative, or mixed.

consensusProxy.title: Public Support Estimate
consensusProxy.text: This is a cautious attempt to gauge broader support. If there’s less data or no polls, the confidence level drops.

howItWorks.title: In Brief: How It Works
howItWorks.description: PolityMarket tracks daily public coverage of Israeli politicians. Every night the system collects articles, posts, and mentions, organizes them, and produces a daily snapshot.
howItWorks.description2: In practice this happens in five simple steps: (1) Collect data from news, Telegram, Reddit, FXP, and Bluesky; (2) Clean noise and irrelevant content; (3) AI reads the material and extracts metrics; (4) A fixed formula computes a 0–10 score; (5) The screen shows two views: media tone, and a public support estimate when there’s enough basis.

scoring.title: How the Score is Built
scoring.description: Each politician has a base score of 0–10. It’s built from 8 domains using a fixed formula. If a particular domain is missing that day, its weight is redistributed among the remaining domains so no one is penalized unfairly. The system then smooths sharp jumps between days. Important: the AI reads the material and returns metrics, but the fixed formula is what determines the final score.
scoring.step1: Collect articles, posts, and public activity related to the politician.
scoring.step2: AI extracts fixed metrics from all the material, such as general tone, presence, and activity.
scoring.step3: The system combines the metrics using fixed weights and smooths the result against recent days.
scoring.policyDesc: Measures how much the public approves the politician’s policy positions, on a scale from total opposition to full support.
scoring.hostilityDesc: Measures how hostile and aggressive the media coverage is. Less hostile coverage means a higher score.
scoring.amplificationDesc: Measures the likelihood that coverage will spread and go viral on social media. A high score means strong media presence.
scoring.formula: In simple terms: each domain gets a weight. If a domain is missing, its weight is split among the rest. The result is a relatively stable 0–10 score that doesn’t flip from every headline.

marketLayer.title: Why There’s Also a 0–100 Scale
marketLayer.description: The internal 0–10 score is good for calculation, but not always easy to read. So the screen stretches the differences to a 0–100 scale, making it easier to see who’s trending up, who’s treading water, and who’s weakening.
marketLayer.rawDescription: This is the score the system calculates behind the scenes. It’s good for internal comparisons and consistency over time.
marketLayer.displayDescription: This is the score you see on screen. 50 is roughly today’s midpoint. This score is designed for easy reading, not to replace the original calculation.
marketLayer.percentile: Daily ranking — each politician and party also gets a relative position compared to everyone else that day.
marketLayer.tiers: Tiers — S, A, B, C are just convenient labels for quick reading. They don’t change the number itself.
marketLayer.delta: Daily change — the arrow shows if the politician went up or down compared to yesterday, and only when there’s a reasonable basis for comparison.
marketLayer.stability: Important to remember — the 0–100 scale is for illustration. The calculation itself stays the same even when the presentation changes.

dimensions.title: 8 Scoring Dimensions
dimensions.publicSentimentDesc: A combination of how supportive or critical the coverage is, how much policy approval there is, and how prominent the politician is in the discourse.
dimensions.parliamentaryActivityDesc: How active the politician is in the Knesset: votes, committees, and bills, based on Open Knesset data.
dimensions.mediaCredibilityDesc: How much the politician’s public statements appear to match available facts.
dimensions.transparencyEthicsDesc: How much the politician is perceived as transparent, accessible, and open to criticism.
dimensions.fieldActivityDesc: How much the politician is seen outside the studio: visits, tours, and field events.
dimensions.satireCulturalImpactDesc: How present the politician is in popular culture, satire shows, and memes. This is a sign of relevance, not a penalty.
dimensions.legislativeQualityDesc: What the politician’s legislative activity looks like, not just how many times they voted.
dimensions.flipflopIndexDesc: How much the politician sticks to what they promised voters, rather than saying one thing then another.
dimensions.agendaBonusDesc: Politicians who lead public discourse can receive a small bonus. This is not a separate category, but a modest addition.

aiAnalysis.title: What the AI Does
aiAnalysis.description: The AI doesn’t just count positive or negative words. It tries to understand context. For example:
aiAnalysis.sarcasm: Detecting when a compliment is actually mockery or cynicism.
aiAnalysis.pdd: Distinguishing between regular criticism and attempts to portray a politician as illegitimate or dangerous.
aiAnalysis.nuance: Understanding irony, Israeli contexts, and implied criticism.

dataSources.title: Where the Data Comes From
dataSources.description: The system relies on a mix of news and social networks:
dataSources.hebrew: Hebrew news — Ynet, Walla, Maariv, Israel Hayom, Globes, Channel 14, Channel 13, Kikar HaShabbat, i24NEWS, TheMarker, and Google News search in Hebrew.
dataSources.english: English news — Times of Israel, Jerusalem Post, i24NEWS, and Google News search in English, for international coverage.
dataSources.social: Social media — Public Telegram channels (Kan News, Abu Ali Express, Galei Tzahal, and more), Reddit (r/Israel, r/worldnews, r/IsraelPolitics), FXP forum, and Bluesky.
dataSources.frequency: Data is updated daily at 02:00 AM (Israel time). Each politician is analyzed based on their headlines and mentions in the last 24 hours.

qualityControl.title: How We Try to Reduce Errors
qualityControl.description: No system is perfect, but there are several safeguards:
qualityControl.validation: Automatic validation — if data is missing or numbers don’t look reasonable, the result is discarded.
qualityControl.drift: Ongoing accuracy checks — the system is regularly compared against manually reviewed samples.
qualityControl.retry: Automatic retry — if a read fails, the system tries again before giving up.
qualityControl.deterministic: Fixed calculation — the same data will always produce the same score, without the AI’s mood changing.

visualization.title: How to Read the Map
visualization.description: Each politician is shown as a block. Its size and color change based on what you’ve chosen to view.
visualization.size: Block size — generally, more coverage = a larger block. You can also switch to size by score.
visualization.color: Block color — red means a weaker position, yellow is roughly in the middle, and green means a stronger position. In public support mode, colors represent that estimate instead of media tone.
visualization.interaction: Clicking a block opens a panel with today’s summary, dimension breakdown, support estimate, and source list.
visualization.displayDescription: In the sidebar you can switch between several display modes to read the data from different angles:
visualization.sizeByVolume: Volume — block size by how much the politician was discussed in the last 24 hours. This is the default.
visualization.sizeByScore: Score — block size by the 0–100 display score, so higher-scoring politicians appear larger.
visualization.colorByScore: Score — block color by relative position: red is weaker, green is stronger. This is the default.
visualization.colorByVolume: Volume — block color by coverage amount: light blue = lots of attention, dark blue = little attention.

general.title: General
general.text: The information, scores, and explanations on PolityMarket are intended for general information, research, and entertainment purposes only. They do not constitute political, legal, financial, academic, or professional advice of any kind.

accuracy.title: Accuracy and Reliability
accuracy.text: The service is based on automated processing of public sources. We do not guarantee the accuracy, completeness, timeliness, or reliability of the data, scores, or explanations. AI analysis may also contain errors, biases, or inaccurate interpretation of source text.

aiLimitations.title: AI Limitations
aiLimitations.text: Analyses are performed by a large language model (LLM). It may miss context, misread sarcasm, or interpret text differently than a human reader. AI models may also reflect linguistic, cultural, or political biases. Scores do not express a personal, editorial, or political position of the service operators.

noEndorsement.title: No Endorsement
noEndorsement.text: The service does not support, promote, or oppose any politician, party, or position. A high or low score is not a recommendation, condemnation, or editorial stance. It is merely the result of automated processing of public coverage.

dataSources.title: Data Sources
dataSources.text: Data is collected from public sources such as news websites, social networks, and RSS feeds. We do not control the content of the sources and are not responsible for their accuracy. A particular source may be temporarily unavailable, which can affect the daily picture.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.text: The service does not collect personally identifiable information from users. Preferences such as favorites and filters are stored in the browser only (localStorage) and are not sent to servers. No tracking cookies are used.

liability.title: Limitation of Liability
liability.text: The service operators shall not be liable for direct, indirect, special, consequential, or punitive damages resulting from use of the service or reliance on its information, including political decisions, investments, or other actions taken on its basis.

changes.title: Changes
changes.text: We may change the calculation method, data sources, update frequency, or any other part of the service at any time without prior notice.

descriptions.Likud: Israel’s dominant right-wing party, in power for most of the past decade — except for the Bennett–Lapid government (2021–2022). Built on Begin’s Revisionist Zionism, it now blends free-market economics with security hawkishness and populism. Under Netanyahu, it reabsorbed Sa’ar and Elkin from HaYamin HaMamlakhti ahead of the 2026 cycle.
descriptions.Yesh Atid: The largest opposition party, founded by journalist Yair Lapid as a centrist alternative. Focuses on middle-class economics, secular civic identity, and rules-based foreign policy. Served as the senior coalition partner in 2021–2022 with Lapid as PM.
descriptions.Blue and White: Re-established in 2026 after the dissolution of National Unity, led by former IDF Chief of Staff Benny Gantz. Positions itself as a centrist security alternative to both Likud and Yesh Atid, leaning on Gantz’s military background.
descriptions.Yashar: Founded in 2025 by former IDF Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot and MK Matan Kahana after leaving National Unity. Emphasizes professional security leadership and centrist pragmatism over party politics.
descriptions.HaMiluimnikim: A one-MK party founded by Yoaz Hendel in 2025 after leaving National Unity. Represents the reservist ethos — economic centrism, security hawkishness, and critical distance from both the right-wing coalition and the traditional opposition.
descriptions.Religious Zionism: A hard-line religious-nationalist party led by Finance Minister Smotrich. Supports West Bank annexation, Torah-based governance, and settlement expansion. A key coalition partner with significant influence on fiscal and Judea & Samaria policy.
descriptions.Otzma Yehudit: An ultra-nationalist party led by National Security Minister Ben Gvir. Rooted in the Kahanist movement, it has been mainstreamed into coalition politics since 2022. Supports aggressive policing, Jewish sovereignty on the Temple Mount, and hardline security policy.
descriptions.Shas: The Mizrahi ultra-Orthodox party, one of the largest Haredi factions. Founded by Rabbi Ovadia Yosef, it combines religious conservatism with social welfare support for the Mizrahi working class. A perennial coalition balancer for decades.
descriptions.United Torah Judaism: An Ashkenazi Haredi alliance uniting Agudat Yisrael and Degel HaTorah. Focuses almost exclusively on preserving Haredi lifestyle — yeshiva study, military exemptions, and religious education funding. A reliable coalition partner for right-wing governments.
descriptions.Yisrael Beiteinu: A secular-nationalist party with strong support among Russian speakers. Under Lieberman, it combines security hawkishness with staunch secularism, opposing both Haredi influence and Arab political power. In opposition since refusing to sit with Haredi parties.
descriptions.Democrats: Founded in 2024 as a merger of Labor and Meretz, led by former IDF deputy chief and MK Yair Golan. Joined by Labor defectors Lazimi, Kariv, and Rayten. Aims to revive social-democratic politics with emphasis on equality, LGBTQ+ rights, and peace support.
descriptions.Labor: Israel’s historic founding party, ruled from 1948 to 1977 and intermittently since. After Merav Michaeli’s departure and key MKs leaving for the Democrats, the party is currently extra-parliamentary and facing an existential crisis ahead of the next elections.
descriptions.Hadash-Ta'al: A joint list of the Arab–Jewish communist Hadash and the Arab-nationalist Ta’al. Represents Arab citizens alongside Jewish left-wing activists. Supports equality, ending the occupation, and full civil rights for Israel’s Arab minority.
descriptions.Ra'am: The political party of the southern branch of the Islamic Movement. Made history in 2021 as the first Arab party to join a coalition, prioritizing pragmatic achievements — budgets, infrastructure, and fighting crime — for Arab communities over ideological purity.
descriptions.Noam: A one-MK ultra-conservative party focused on opposing LGBTQ+ rights, liberal curricula, and what it calls ‘Western cultural erosion.’ Briefly held a deputy minister role in the current coalition before internal friction.
descriptions.HaYamin HaMamlakhti: Originally founded by Gideon Sa’ar after splitting from Likud. After Sa’ar and Elkin returned to Likud in 2025, the remaining MKs — Sharren Haskel, Michel Buskila, and Akram Hasson — continue as a coalition faction with a national-liberal, law-and-order platform.
descriptions.Bennett 2026: Former PM Naftali Bennett’s comeback vehicle, registered in April 2025 after years out of politics. Positions itself as a pragmatic right-wing alternative to Netanyahu, leaning on Bennett’s high-tech background and brief PM tenure in 2021–2022.
descriptions.El HaDegel: A small Religious Zionist faction led by Matan Yafe, positioned between mainstream Religious Zionism and the Kahanist right. Focuses on settlement support and religious-nationalist values.

quickAbout.title: What am I looking at?
quickAbout.line1: A daily status map of Israeli politics, based on what’s been publicly published.
quickAbout.line2: We collect news coverage and public posts, and update the picture every night at 02:00.
quickAbout.line3: There are two modes: Media Tone shows how the politician is being discussed right now; Public Support is a broader, more cautious estimate.
quickAbout.line4: Bigger block = more attention. Green = relatively strong position. Red = relatively weak position.
